Learning Objectives
Determine medical optimization for early fracture management in geriatric orthopaedic
patients.
Review delirium prevention in geriatric orthopaedic patients.
Describe fall risk assessment and prevention for geriatric orthopaedic patients.
Introduction
Physiologic Considerations
Special consideration is required for geriatric orthopaedic patients because of their physiologic
decline and diminished functional reserve, often in combination with considerable


Physiologic Considerations
The numerous physiologic changes associated with aging in combination with
comorbidities complicate the recognition of injury severity, compromise the body’s
response to trauma, and predispose the body to the development of complications.1
Age-related organ system changes are described in Table 1.2,3 Changes in the central
nervous system often result in increased delirium, postoperative cognitive decline, and
sensitivity to anesthetic agents or opioids. Elderly patients have decreased muscle mass,
chest wall recoil, and cough strength, all of which contribute to increased risks of
aspiration, atelectasis, and pneumonia. The effect of aging on the cardiovascular system
is profound in trauma patients. Older patients exhibit a blunted chronotropic response
that may be exacerbated by pharmacologic beta-blockade or other rate-controlling
agents. These patients cannot augment cardiac output and compensate for hemorrhage
by increasing systemic vascular resistance. Vital signs that are interpreted as normal in
young patients may reflect relative hypotension and decreased end-organ perfusion in
elderly patients, particularly in those with baseline hypertension. Although hypotension
is defined as a systolic blood pressure of less than 90 mm Hg in younger trauma
patients, systolic blood pressures of less than 110 mm Hg are associated with increased
mortality in elderly trauma patients.4 The proliferation of anticoagulation for
arrhythmias and thromboembolic disease has resulted in an increasing number of
elderly patients presenting with coagulopathy. Because of impaired thermoregulation,
elderly patients may present with hypothermia despite being found indoors. Although
the degree of temperature derangement is not as profound as with environmental
exposure, hypothermia complicates and worsens trauma outcomes in elderly patients.5
In combination, these changes create a complex physiologic condition. Orthopaedic
surgeons who specialize in the treatment of geriatric patients must understand these
physiologic changes. These changes must be considered in geriatric patients undergoing
the acute stress of injury, anesthesia, and surgical fixation (Table 1).

Epidemiology
Fragility fracture is an epidemic problem worldwide.
Fragility fractures are defined as fractures that result from a fall from a standing height or less
or in the absence of trauma.6

Epidemiology

3/30

Osteoporotic fractures, also known as fragility fractures, are an epidemic problem
worldwide given the rapidly increasing elderly population. Fragility fractures can occur at
multiple skeletal sites, most often at the spine, hip, or wrist, and cause substantial
morbidity and mortality.7 The US population 50 years and older is predicted to increase
by 60% between 2000 and 2025, reaching 121.3 million individuals, with those older than
85 years representing the fastest-growing segment of the population.8 The projected
increase in the elderly US population will lead to an increasingly frail population at
greater risk for falls and fractures.
Perioperative Management
Multidisciplinary Approach
Use an interdisciplinary team approach to optimize outcomes of early fracture repair.
Avoid unnecessary tests and unnecessary specialist consultation.

Multidisciplinary Approach
The preoperative medical assessment is meant to risk-stratify the patient, improve
reversible acute medical abnormalities, and prevent complications.9 An interdisciplinary
team approach (including orthopaedics, geriatrics, or internal medicine/hospitalist/family
medicine, anesthesiology, nursing, and therapists) is especially important in achieving
the best outcomes. The team approach should minimize unnecessary preoperative tests
and consultations to avoid unnecessary delay and expense.10
Timing of Management
The goal is for surgical repair to be as safe as possible in a timely manner (ideally within 24 to
48 hours after fracture).


Timing of Management
After the decision to proceed with surgical repair has been made, the goal of the
preoperative medical assessment is to promptly make surgical repair as safe as possible.
Timely surgical treatment decreases patient discomfort and morbidity and facilitates
expedient rehabilitation for ambulation, which helps patients to return to their baseline
function quickly and safely.11-13 Preoperatively, patients are bedridden and in
considerable pain. Unnecessary delays in surgical repair result in prolonged
immobilization, increased complications, and increased morbidity and mortality. For
patients with a hip fracture, early surgical repair was shown to reduce mortality and
morbidity in a population-based cohort study.14-18
Medical Optimization
Medical optimization includes adequate hydration, pain control, cognition assessment,
delirium mitigation, and reversal of coagulopathy if applicable.
Hydration
Adequate volume resuscitation is necessary to avoid additional complications, such as
intraoperative hypotension and acute kidney injury.

Hydration
Most patients with a hip fracture are dehydrated or volume depleted to some extent on
presentation, often because of bleeding at the fracture site or limited oral intake after
the fall. The physiologic stress response to trauma induces inflammation, catabolism,
and intravascular volume depletion.9 Fluid resuscitation and maintenance are among
the most important facets of managing critically ill patients admitted for surgical
treatment. The amount of intravenous hydration is based on clinical judgment; however,
typically, isotonic saline can be started at 100 to 200 mL/h to replete intravascular
volume.19 The patient should be brought to the operating room in a euvolemic state

because this reduces the hemodynamic effects caused by the induction of anesthesia.20
Avoiding intraoperative hypotension has been proposed to improve outcomes in elderly
patients.21 If a patient is hypervolemic postoperatively, the target should be to allow for
cautious excretion of sodium and water.22
Pain Control
Control pain with the use of small doses of narcotics and avoid excessive sedation.

Pain Control
Proper pain management not only is humane but also may reduce the risk of delirium.23
Pain control is best accomplished via small doses of narcotics (eg, 1- to 2-mg doses of
intravenous morphine or oral narcotic medications, such as 5 mg of oxycodone).
Narcotics can be titrated to achieve the desired effect. In patients with renal or hepatic
insufficiency, hydromorphone is the preferred narcotic agent.9 The use of traction is not
helpful with regard to pain relief in patients with most types of hip fractures and may
contribute to pressure ulceration.15 Effective pain control must be achieved without
excessive sedation.
Anemia and Transfusions
Consider blood transfusions in patients with a preoperative hemoglobin level less than 8 g/dL.

Anemia and Transfusions
Hemoglobin levels should be assessed to ensure that the patient does not require a
blood transfusion preoperatively. In a prospective randomized trial of 2,016 patients
with a hip fracture, Carson et al24 reported that a liberal transfusion strategy
(hemoglobin threshold of 10 g/dL) compared with a restrictive transfusion strategy

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003009
6/30

(symptoms of anemia or at physician discretion for a hemoglobin level of <8 g/dL) did
not reduce the death rate, inability to walk independently within 60-day follow-up, or in-
hospital morbidity in elderly patients with high cardiovascular risk. Blood transfusions
should be considered in patients with a preoperative hemoglobin level of less than 8
g/dL because it likely represents a risk to a patient who will incur surgical blood loss,
leading to an additional decrease in hemoglobin level.24,25
Coagulopathies
The treatment of patients with a markedly elevated international normalized ratio (INR) is
controversial; however, the use of vitamin K has been shown to be safe and effective.
Recent studies suggest that surgical treatment should not be delayed in patients with a hip
fracture being treated with direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs) on admission.26
Delayed surgical treatment in patients being treated with antiplatelet agents (aspirin,
clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel) is not recommended because it is associated with an
increased overall mortality rate.

Coagulopathies
The prothrombin time/INR should be assessed because patients may be being treated
via chronic anticoagulation therapy or have a condition affecting coagulation, such as
liver disease. Vitamin K antagonists, such as warfarin, are widely used, with multiple
clinical indications. The treatment of patients with a markedly elevated INR is
controversial and complicated by the acute need for the patient to undergo surgical
fixation.9 A study showed that active management to reverse anticoagulation
preoperatively may facilitate earlier surgical management without increasing
complications.27 The American College of Chest Physicians recommends that the dosing
of vitamin K should be based on a patient’s current INR and risk of bleeding.28
Pharmacologic reversal of warfarin-associated coagulopathy via a combination of
vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma appears to be a safe method to optimize patients for
surgical fixation of hip fractures and is associated with a shorter delay to surgical
treatment in patients with an elevated preoperative INR.29

The use of DOACs is increasing.30 Indications include management and prophylaxis of
deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism and prevention of systemic
embolization in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.31 Patients being treated with the use of
DOACs have increased delays to surgical treatment compared with patients without
anticoagulation or not being treated with the use of vitamin K antagonists. The mean
time to surgical treatment for patients with a hip fracture who are being treated with the
use of DOACs ranges from 35 hours to 66.9 hours.32 Common practice is to withhold
DOACs for 24 to 48 hours, after which surgical treatment can be performed;33 however,
a recent study suggested that delayed surgical treatment is not necessary in patients
with a hip fracture who are being treated with the use of DOACs on admission because
patients who underwent early surgical treatment had no increase in hemoglobin level
loss, transfusion rates, or mortality.34 Evidence-based guidelines on urgent surgical
treatment in patients being treated with the use of DOACs are still lacking, and the
risk/benefit decisions with regard to surgical delay and anticoagulation reversal should
remain a multidisciplinary decision.
The use of combined antithrombotic drugs has increased.35 Approximately 3% of
patients with a hip fracture are being treated via dual antiplatelet therapy.36 In general,
aspirin and clopidogrel have been widely used in patients with coronary artery disease,
cerebellar vascular disease, and peripheral artery disease. Newer agents (ticagrelor and
prasugrel) are indicated in patients post–percutaneous coronary intervention. Although
the clinical tendency is to delay surgical treatment in patients being treated via dual
antiplatelet therapy, delaying surgical management because of these antiplatelet agents
is associated with an increased overall mortality rate.37,38 No difference in bleeding
complications, blood loss, or transfusion requirements was noted in patients with a hip
fracture who were being treated with the use of aspirin and clopidogrel compared with
those not being treated with the use of antiplatelets.38,39 The thromboembolic and
infectious complications were substantially higher in the delayed surgical group, further
supporting the need for early surgical treatment despite antiplatelet therapy.40
Cardiopulmonary Evaluation

Four major clinical predictors of increased perioperative cardiovascular risk include unstable
acute coronary syndrome, decompensated heart failure, substantial arrhythmia, and severe
valvular disease.41
Patients with an exercise capacity of 4 or more metabolic equivalents (METs) without
symptoms should undergo planned surgical treatment.41
The routine use of echocardiography is associated with delay surgical treatment and should be
avoided if not clinically indicated. The indications for echocardiography are listed in Table 2.41
Preoperative pulmonary evaluation (including pulmonary function tests) does not predict
respiratory complications in nonelective surgical management.9,42


Cardiopulmonary Evaluation
Preoperative cardiac evaluation should be tailored to the assumption that patients
require early surgical treatment.9 This evaluation aims to diagnose and manage possible
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:55 AM
AAOS | Treatment of Geriatric Orthopaedic Patients
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003009
9/30

absolute contraindications to surgical management. The American Heart Association
recognizes four major clinical predictors of increased perioperative cardiovascular risk:
unstable acute coronary syndrome, decompensated heart failure, substantial
arrhythmia, and severe valvular disease.41 Based on current scientific guidelines,
patients with an exercise capacity of 4 or more METs without symptoms should undergo
planned surgical treatment.41 This determination is made by asking patients about their
activity level. At 4 METs, a patient can ascend a flight of stairs, walk a block at 4 mph, run
a short distance, or perform heavy housework without shortness of breath or chest pain.
The routine use of echocardiography is associated with delayed surgical management
and should be avoided if not clinically indicated.41 Table 2 lists comorbidities that
require preoperative cardiac assessment.41 Only unstable conditions warrant delayed
surgical management.
Postoperative pulmonary complications may occur in as many 50% of patients with
chronic pulmonary disease. Preoperative pulmonary evaluation (including pulmonary
function tests) does not predict respiratory complications in nonelective surgical
management.9,42 Steroids and bronchodilators may be indicated in patients with chronic
lung diseases, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; however, the risk of
arrhythmia or myocardial ischemia from beta-agonists must be considered. Respiratory
infections should be managed as soon as possible because they may substantially affect
outcomes.9
Cognitive Assessment and Delirium Prevention
Common components of successful delirium prevention programs include adequately
controlling pain, encouraging early mobilization, performing frequent reorientation,
addressing malnourishment, avoiding dehydration, managing sleep disorders, managing
vision and hearing impairment, assessing bowel/bladder function, reviewing medications,
consulting geriatric medicine, and training facility staff.43


Cognitive Assessment and Delirium Prevention
Delirium is a frequently encountered complication in geriatric orthopaedic patients;
however, it receives much less attention compared with other complications.44 Because
of elevated levels of frailty, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, and coexisting cognitive
impairment, patients with a hip fracture have at a particularly elevated risk for delirium,
with prevalence rates as high as 61% in the perioperative period.45-48 Postoperative
delirium is associated with a prolonged hospital stay, discharge to a care home, difficulty
in regaining function in activities of daily living, and increased risk of cognitive
dysfunction and dementia in the future.49,50 In the general population of frail, older
adults, patients with delirium have poorer functional status, and fewer of these patients
can return home.51-53
Several underlying causes predispose geriatric patients with a hip fracture to
perioperative delirium.43 Known risk factors for postoperative delirium include
modifiable factors, such as the use of physical restraints, opioids, polypharmacy,
indwelling urinary catheters, active infection, and the number of hours immobilized.54,55
Timely and corrective management of these underlying causes and patient comorbidities
may decrease perioperative delirium in elderly patients with a fracture. Surgeons must
recognize cognitive problems because cognitive impairment has the strongest
association with delirium during the hospital stay. A confusion assessment method56
(Resource 1) and some form of mental status testing will help to determine this status.
The short-form mini-mental test57 and the mini-cognitive test58 are good examples of
short tests to assess for dementia.59
To prevent delirium, a team approach should be taken. Adequately controlling pain,
encouraging early mobilization, performing frequent reorientation, addressing
malnourishment, avoiding dehydration, enhancing sleep, using appropriate vision and
hearing aids, assessing bowel/bladder function, reviewing medications, consulting
geriatric medicine, and training facility staff have been shown to be effective.43

Anesthesia
No known difference in mortality exists between neuraxial blocks and general anesthesia.
Conflicting results have been reported in association with the type of anesthesia and the risk
of acute postoperative confusion.

Anesthesia
Death after hip fracture management occurs in 17% to 37% of older patients within the
first year, and one modifiable factor is the effect of anesthesia.60,61 The ideal anesthesia
technique for this patient population has yet to be defined. Many studies have been
performed to determine whether one technique is better than another; however, no
differences have been found between techniques in the current literature.62,63 Neuman
et al63 reported that, among patients undergoing hip repair, the use of regional
anesthesia compared with general anesthesia was not associated with lower 30-day
mortality but was associated with a modestly shorter hospital length of stay. A recent
review of 11 trials that included 2,152 participants suggested no difference in 30-day
mortality, pneumonia, myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular accident, congestive heart
failure, acute kidney injury, pulmonary embolism, number of patients who received
transfusion of red blood cells, length of surgery, length of hospital stay, and the risk of
DVT between neuraxial blocks and general anesthesia.64 Conflicting results exist with
regard to whether regional anesthesia compared with general anesthesia is associated
with a decreased risk of acute postoperative confusion. A recent review of patients with
a hip fracture reported no evidence to suggest that anesthesia type influences
postoperative delirium.65 Another literature review, which included 3,611 patients,
assessed related factors of delirium after orthopaedic surgery and reported that the
highest postoperative delirium rate was associated with general anesthesia (6.50%)
compared to 0.77% after spinal anesthesia and 0.47% after local anesthesia (P < 0.001).66
Another literature review reported that the use of a multimodal analgesic regimen,
including liposome bupivacaine, may extend the time to first postsurgical opioid use.67
Various results from previous studies generate uncertainty with regard to the best type

of anesthesia for elderly and fragile patients. High-quality trials are necessary to
reevaluate the effect of the anesthetic technique in this patient population.
Postoperative Considerations
DVT Prophylaxis
Low-molecular-weight heparin or DOACs as the initial agents; however, DOACs should be
avoided in patients with a hip fracture.
For those with severe renal insufficiency, unfractionated heparin is the preferred prophylactic
agent.
Aspirin can be used after a short course (eg, 5 days) of an initial agent.

DVT Prophylaxis
The American College of Chest Physicians and the American Society of Hematology have
stated the recommendations for DVT prophylaxis in orthopaedic surgery patients.68,69
The risk of postoperative DVT and pulmonary embolism in orthopaedic patients is
among the highest of all surgical specialties. The risk of postoperative DVT/pulmonary
embolism and bleeding in orthopaedic patients depends on procedure- and patient-
related risk factors, which must be assessed. Patient-related risk factors for
DVT/pulmonary embolism include patients older than 75 years of age (particularly ≥85
years), poor preoperative ambulation, obesity, and cardiovascular disease.70,71 Hip and
knee arthroplasty, hip fracture surgery, pelvic and multiple fractures, and postoperative
cast immobilization are considered risks for DVT.
In patients with an elevated risk of DVT but a minimal risk of bleeding, current
recommendations are low-molecular-weight heparin or DOACs (preferably rivaroxaban
or apixaban rather than dabigatran or edoxaban because of fewer drug interactions) as
initial agents. In patients with severe renal insufficiency, unfractionated heparin is the
preferred alternative to low-molecular-weight heparin and DOACs.68,69 Warfarin often is
used in patients who were being treated with the use of warfarin before fracture. Aspirin
is less well supported by data as an initial agent for DVT prophylaxis; however, switching

to aspirin after a short course (eg, 5 days) of rivaroxaban may be suitable in low-risk
patients. Similar principles for agent selection must be used in patients undergoing
surgical treatment for a hip fracture; however, because DOACs have not been evaluated
in patients undergoing surgical treatment for a hip fracture, their use should be avoided
in this patient population.68
Importantly, the clinician should be aware that DVT prophylaxis reduces, but does not
entirely eliminate, the risk of DVT. In addition, DVT prophylaxis has a greater effect on
reducing the rate of asymptomatic events rather than symptomatic events and has
minimal effect on mortality. In high-risk patients, pharmacologic prophylaxis should be
administered for a minimum of 10 to 14 days postopertively and for a maximum of 35
days postoperatively.68,69
Nutrition
Higher nutritional intake is associated with fewer postoperative complications, improved
rehabilitation, reduced pressure sores, and improved muscle strength.
A multidisciplinary approach is required to reduce malnourishment.

Nutrition
Nearly one-half of elderly patients with a hip fracture are malnourished, which is a risk
factor for poor outcomes.72,73 As a part of the American College of Surgeons National
Surgical Quality Improvement Program, a retrospective cohort study of geriatric patients
(≥65 years of age) who underwent surgical treatment for a hip fracture showed that
hypoalbuminemia was a substantial independent risk factor for mortality
postoperatively.73,74 Nutritional intervention is cost-effective and is associated with
improved nutritional status and great functional recovery.75 A multidisciplinary
approach is required to reduce malnourishment in geriatric orthopaedic patients.76
Having a team that includes a dietitian and nurses trained in nutrition also is associated
with better outcomes.76

Osteoporosis Assessment
Bone mineral density assessment is recommended for all women 65 years or older and men
who have manifestation of low bone mass (low trauma fractures or loss of height) or risks for
fracture.
Surgeons must identify patients with a recent fracture as high-risk patients because a recent
fracture is associated with an increased risk for a second fracture.

Osteoporosis Assessment
The prevalence of osteoporosis in the United States is estimated to increase from
approximately 10 million to more than 14 million individuals in 2020 (based on 2000
census data).77 Osteoporosis or osteopenia largely is unmanaged and silent until a
fracture occurs.78 Bone mineral density assessment is recommended for all women 65
years or older and men who have manifestations of low bone mass (low trauma
fractures or loss of height) or risks for fracture (such as glucocorticoid therapy, androgen
deprivation therapy, hyperthyroidism, low body weight, hypogonadism, previous fragility
fracture).79,80 Surgeons must identify patients with a recent fracture as high-risk patients
because a recent fracture is associated with a high risk for a second fracture within the
first 2 years after the first fracture.81-83 A recent study showed that zoledronate,
alendronate, risedronate, etidronate, ibandronate, parathyroid hormone, denosumab,
and selective estrogen receptor modulators had substantial secondary prevention
effects on osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture.84
The Fracture Risk Assessment Tool, a computer-based algorithm developed by the World
Health Organization Collaborating Centre for Metabolic Bone Diseases first released in
2008, is a tool designed to predict fracture risk by combining risk factors for reduced
bone quality and includes an optional field for measurement of bone mineral density
(Resource 2). In the United States, patients with a 10-year hip fracture risk of 3% or
greater or a major osteoporotic fracture risk of 20% or more should undergo treatment
for osteoporosis.85,86

Assessment for osteoporosis should include additional laboratory tests to assess for
secondary causes, particularly in those with a fragility fracture.9 Serum calcium level,
estimated glomerular filtration rate, 25-hydroxy vitamin D level, intact parathyroid
hormone level, thyrotropin level, and testosterone level (for men) should be included in
the osteoporosis assessment.79
Management of Osteoporosis
A daily intake of 1,200-mg of calcium and vitamin D supplements is recommended.
Preferred management includes antiresorptive therapy, anabolic agents, and selective
estrogen receptor modulators.
Counseling should be provided to encourage weight-bearing activities, smoking cessation, fall
prevention, medication compliance, and activity modifications.

Management of Osteoporosis
The goal of osteoporosis management is to maintain bone mass, limit bone loss, and
decrease fracture risk. The currently available osteoporosis treatment options are
antiresorptive (inhibiting the osteoclasts, such as diphosphonates, receptor activator of
nuclear factor-kappa B ligand antibodies, and selective estrogen receptor modulators),
bone-forming (stimulating the osteoblasts, such as teriparatide and abaloparatide), or
dual-acting (simultaneously stimulating the osteoblasts and inhibiting the osteoclasts,
such as romosozumab).87
In patients newly diagnosed with osteoporosis, initial treatment likely will be an
antiresorptive treatment, such as a diphosphonate or denosumab.88 Patients treated
with the use of diphosphonates may be evaluated for the appropriateness of treatment
discontinuation if treated via oral or intravenously administrated diphosphonates for 5
or 3 years, respectively. Based on the outcome of the FLEX and HORIZON studies,
treatment discontinuation should not be considered in patients with a hip bone mineral
density T score less than -2.5, prevalent vertebral fractures, or nonvertebral fractures
during treatment.89,90 Patients treated via denosumab should continue treatment

9/4/26, 10:55 AM
AAOS | Treatment of Geriatric Orthopaedic Patients
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003009
16/30

because a rebound activation of bone turnover and subsequent bone loss is likely if
denosumab is discontinued.91
Regardless of the management of osteoporosis, all patients require adequate calcium
and vitamin D intake.9 The National Academy of Sciences recommends a daily intake of
1,200 mg of calcium in adults older than 50 years.92 Vitamin D supplements should be
administered to maintain a serum 25-hydroxy vitamin D level of 32 ng/mL (75 nmol/L) or
higher. Vitamin D is important for not only bone strength and mineralization but also
lower extremity muscle strength, gait speed and performance, and balance in individuals
older than 65 years.93 Vitamin D also reduces the risk of falls in the geriatric
population.94
Counseling should be provided to all patients to encourage weight-bearing activities,
smoking cessation, fall prevention, and activity modifications to minimize the risk of
future fracture.95 A national program called “Own the Bone” is a web-based, evidence-
based quality-improvement initiative developed by the American Orthopaedic
Association to improve diagnosis and medical management after a fragility fracture. The
ultimate goal of this program is to change physician and patient behavior to positively
affect osteoporosis management and to reduce the incidence of future fractures. The
program provides extensive educational materials and guidance for the development of
a comprehensive program to improve osteoporosis management after fragility
fracture.96,97
Fall Risk Assessment and Fall Prevention
Current guidelines specify that primary care providers should screen older adults for falls and
the risk for falling at least once per year by asking about falls and unsteadiness when walking.
Three key risk factors (balance, medications, and home safety) should be addressed in all
individuals at high fall risk.
Patients should be referred to clinical and community resources to address modifiable risk
factors for falls.


Fall Risk Assessment and Fall Prevention
Approximately 30% of individuals older than 65 years and 50% of individuals older than
80 years fall each year.97 Approximately 50% of residents in long-term care settings fall
each year, and approximately 10% of community-dwelling individuals 75 years or older
without risk factors fall during any given year.98
Fall risk factors can be categorized as intrinsic or environmental. Intrinsic factors include
age-related physiologic changes, such as cognitive deficits, gait, decreased muscle
strength, increased postural sway, slowed righting reflexes, decreased step height,
decreased proprioception, balance deficits, and vision impairment. Environmental
factors include medications, footwear, assistive devices, home features, alcohol and
drugs, and support from caregivers.99,100 Fall assessment and fall risk reduction are
important in fracture prevention.
Helping patients understand the importance of intrinsic factors in causing falls is
important because older individuals frequently underestimate their risk of falling.101,102
The American Geriatrics Society and the British Geriatrics Society published a clinical
practice guideline on fall risk screening, assessment, and management.103,104 The
guideline recommends annual fall risk screening for all adults 65 years or older. This
screening consists of asking patients if they have fallen two or more times in the past
year or sought medical attention for a fall. If patients have not fallen, they should be
asked if they feel unsteady when walking. Patients who answer “yes” to any of these
questions have an increased risk for falls and should undergo additional assessment.105
Individuals who have fallen once without injury should undergo evaluation of balance
and gait; those with gait or balance abnormalities should undergo additional
assessment.103,104 A history of one fall without injury and gait or balance problems does
not warrant additional assessment beyond continued annual fall risk screening.103,104
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention developed an algorithm that shows
each step of screening and assessment. It also guides treatment options based on an
individual’s level of risk.105,106 This algorithm is part of a tool kit called Stopping Elderly

Accidents, Deaths, and Injuries.107 The algorithm highlights that individuals at minimal
risk (no history of falls, no problems with gait or balance) may benefit from a primary
prevention approach, namely education about fall risk factors, strength and balance
exercises, and vitamin D supplementation.108
One of the critical aspects of risk assessment is a medication review. Several classes of
medications, such as antidepressants, antipsychotics, sedative hypnotics,
benzodiazepines, antihypertensives, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and
diuretics, increase fall risk. Psychoactive medications are independent predictors of
falls.109,110 These medications tend to be sedating, alter sensorium, and impair balance
and gait. Other medications (eg, antihypertensives, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory
drugs, diuretics) are weakly associated with falls.111
Identifying and modifying environmental factors is an effective intervention in a
comprehensive multifactorial approach to preventing falls.104 An environmental
assessment typically is conducted by a trained health professional (eg, occupational
therapist). The intention of the assessment is to identify hazardous conditions in the
home, such as obstacles in pathways or on stairs, ill-fitting footwear, unsuitable assistive
devices, inadequate lighting, and slippery surfaces. It also identifies hazards outside the
home, such as cracked pavement or sloped yards.104
Finally, special consideration is necessary for patients with dementia. Dementia impairs
gait, balance, and hazard recognition. Patients with dementia have a disproportionately
high rate of falls and fractures and poorer outcomes.112 As many as 50% to 80% of
patients with dementia fall within 12 months.113,114 Evidence suggests fall prevention
interventions, which include strength, balance, and endurance/mobility training that
progress in intensity over time, may improve mobility and balance deficits and aid in the
reduction of falls in patients with dementia. The program can be undertaken at home, in
a group at a community center, or in a gymnasium.115,116

The goal is to make surgical repair as safe as possible in a timely manner (ideally within 24 to
48 hours after fracture).
Avoid unnecessary tests or specialist consultations to avoid delay if not clinically indicated.
Adequate volume resuscitation is necessary to avoid additional complications, such as
intraoperative hypotension and acute kidney injury.
The treatment of patients with a markedly elevated INR is controversial; however, the use of
vitamin K is safe and effective. Fresh frozen plasma should be used for urgent cases.
Surgical treatment should not be delayed in patients with a hip fracture who are being treated
with the use of DOACs on admission.
Delayed surgical management of a hip fracture in patients being treated with the use of
antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel) is not recommended.
Patients with an exercise capacity of 4 or more METs without symptoms should undergo
planned surgical treatment.
The routine use of echocardiography should be avoided.
Common components of successful delirium prevention programs
Adequately controlling pain
Encouraging early mobilization
Performing frequent reorientation
Addressing malnourishment
Avoiding dehydration
Managing sleep disorders
Managing vision and hearing impairment
Assessing bowel/bladder function
Reviewing medications
Consulting geriatric medicine
Training facility staff
Low-molecular-weight heparin or DOACs (preferably avoid in patients with a hip fracture) are
preferred initial agents for DVT prophylaxis (unfractionated heparin is the preferred option for
patients with impaired kidneys).
Surgeons must identify patients with a recent fracture as high-risk patients because a recent
fracture is associated with an increased risk of a second fracture.
Current guidelines specify that primary care providers should screen older adults for falls and
risk for falls at least once per year by asking about falls and unsteadiness when walking.
Three key risk factors (balance, medications, and home safety) should be addressed in all
individuals with an elevated risk for falls.
